title: Unions and Narrowing
summary: Accept several types with a union, then narrow it with typeof, truthiness, in, instanceof, and Array.isArray before you use the value.
intro: Real data rarely has one fixed shape. An id can be a number or a string, a name can be missing, and a list of tags can arrive as one string. A union type says exactly which shapes are allowed, and narrowing is how your code finds out which one it has before it uses the value.

steps.title: Union types
steps.body:
A union type lists the types a value may have, joined by `|`. A variable typed `string | number` can hold either one:

```typescript
let code: string | number = 404;
console.log(code.toString()); // 404
code = "NOT_FOUND";
console.log(code.toString()); // NOT_FOUND
```

Until you check which type you have, you can only use what every member of the union has. Strings and numbers both have `toString()`, and `String(value)` and template literals accept any value, so those work right away. `toUpperCase()` exists only on strings, so calling it on a `string | number` is a type error.

Arrays can hold unions too. Put the union in parentheses: `(string | number)[]` is an array whose items are each a string or a number. Without them, `string | number[]` means one string or an array of numbers.

examples.title: IDs
examples.prompt: Format order ids from two systems: the old one stored numbers, the new one stores strings.
examples.explanation: `String(id)` turns either kind of id into a string, so `padStart(6, "0")` can pad it with zeros to 6 characters. The checker accepts this without knowing which kind `id` is, because `String` takes any value. `123456` is already 6 characters long, so it prints unchanged.

examples.title: Only shared members
examples.prompt: Call a string method on the id before checking what it is.
examples.output:
main.ts(2,13): error TS2339: Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'.
  Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'number'.
examples.explanation: `id` might be a number, and numbers have no `toUpperCase`, so the checker reports TS2339 at line 2. The indented line under the error names the member of the union that lacks the method. The program never runs. To call `toUpperCase`, the function has to check that `id` is a string first, which is what narrowing does.

examples.title: Arrays of unions
examples.prompt: Build CSV rows whose cells are a mix of text and numbers.
examples.explanation: `(string | number)[]` lets each cell be either type, and `push` checks every argument against that union, so `cells.push(true)` would be a type error. `join(",")` turns every item into text, numbers included, so the cells need no checks before they print. The loop prints them 3 at a time, one row per person.

practice.title: Quantities
practice.prompt:
Stock counts arrive as numbers from the barcode scanner and as text from a spreadsheet. Print them all the same way.

1. Export `formatQuantity(q: number | string): string`.
2. Return the quantity, a space, and `pcs`, like `12 pcs`.
3. The starter already prints the quantities `12`, `"7"`, and `0`.

Expected output:

```text
12 pcs
7 pcs
0 pcs
```
hints: A template literal accepts strings and numbers alike, so `q` needs no check here.

steps.title: Narrowing with typeof and truthiness

examples.title: Pixels with typeof
examples.prompt: Convert a size to pixels when it comes as a number or as text like `24px`.
examples.explanation: Inside the `if`, the first bubble shows `size` as a `string`, so `Number.parseInt` accepts it. `Number.parseInt(text, 10)` reads base 10 digits from the start of the text and stops at the first character that isn't one, so `"24px"` gives 24 and `"1.5em"` gives 1. The `if` returns, so on the last line only `number` is left, as the second bubble shows, and returning `size` matches the return type.

examples.title: Truthiness and its trap
examples.prompt: Greet a name that may be missing, then watch a truthiness check mistake a stock count of 0 for a missing count.
examples.output:
Hello, Ada!
Hello, guest!
Hello, guest!
mugs: not counted
mugs: 0
plates: not counted
examples.explanation: `if (name)` is false for `null`, `undefined`, and `""`, so all three get the guest greeting, which is what you want for a name. In `stockLine`, `!count` is true for `undefined` and also for `0`, so 0 mugs prints as not counted. `fixedStockLine` compares with `undefined` directly, so 0 counts as a real number and only the plates, with no count at all, print `not counted`.

examples.title: Early return
examples.prompt: Show a badge for the signed-in user, or `guest` when nobody is signed in.
examples.explanation: After `if (user === null)` returns, `user` can only be a `User`, as the bubble shows, so reading `user.name` and `user.plan` needs no second check. Handling the odd case first and returning keeps the main path of the function short and unindented.

practice.title: Normalize quantity
practice.prompt:
Quantities reach the warehouse three ways: the scanner sends numbers, a web form sends text, and a missing value is `null`. Turn each one into a whole number.

1. Export `normalizeQty(q: number | string | null): number`.
2. Return `0` for `null`.
3. Read a string with `Number.parseInt(q, 10)`, and return `0` when that gives `NaN`.
4. Round a number down with `Math.floor`.
5. The starter already prints the results for `4.7`, `"12 boxes"`, `"none"`, and `null`.

Expected output:

```text
4
12
0
0
```
hints: Handle `null` first, then check `typeof q === "string"`. Whatever reaches the end is a number.
Check the parsed value with `Number.isNaN` before you return it.
After the string branch returns, `Math.floor(q)` type-checks, because only `number` is left.

steps.title: in, instanceof, and Array.isArray
steps.body:
`typeof` tells primitives apart, but objects, arrays, and `null` are all `"object"` to it. Narrow objects by what makes each member of the union different:

- `"swim" in animal` is true when the object has a `swim` property, so it narrows to the members that have one.
- `value instanceof Date` checks which class made the object, so it narrows to that class.
- `Array.isArray(input)` is true only for arrays, so it narrows to the array member of a union.

A ternary narrows the same way an `if` does:

```typescript
function message(problem: Error | string): string {
  return problem instanceof Error ? problem.message : problem;
}
console.log(message(new Error("disk full"))); // disk full
console.log(message("timeout")); // timeout
```

examples.title: Fish or bird with in
examples.prompt: Move a fish or a bird by calling whichever method it has.
examples.output:
Nemo swims away
Tweety flies off
examples.explanation: Only `Fish` has a `swim` property, so inside `if ("swim" in animal)` the checker narrows `animal` to `Fish`, and `animal.swim()` is allowed. After that branch returns, only `Bird` is left, so `animal.fly()` type-checks. Both types have `name`, so `animal.name` works everywhere.

examples.title: Dates with instanceof
examples.prompt: Print a delivery date that is either a `Date` or text someone typed.
examples.explanation: `new Date("2026-10-01T09:00:00Z")` builds a date from a timestamp, and `toISOString()` writes it back as `2026-10-01T09:00:00.000Z`, so its first 10 characters are the date. `value instanceof Date` narrows `value` to `Date`, which is why `toISOString` is allowed. Text skips the `if`, and the function returns it as it is.

examples.title: One or many with Array.isArray
examples.prompt: Accept one item or a list of items, and always hand back a list.
examples.explanation: `Array.isArray(input)` narrows `input` to `string[]` inside the `if`, so the function returns it as it is. After the `if`, `input` is a `string`, and `[input]` wraps it in an array of one. Callers always get a `string[]`, so `length` and `join` work without any checks.

practice.title: Flexible tags
practice.prompt:
Posts store their tags three ways: a comma-separated string from an old form, an array from the new editor, or `null` when a post has none. Turn all three into one clean list.

1. Export `normalizeTags(input: string | string[] | null): string[]`.
2. Return an empty array for `null`.
3. Split a string on commas.
4. Trim every tag and make it lowercase.
5. The starter already prints the results for `"TypeScript, Node ,Tips"`, `[" News", "RELEASES "]`, and `null`, each joined with `|` inside square brackets.

Expected output:

```text
[typescript|node|tips]
[news|releases]
[]
```
hints: Handle `null` first. Then `Array.isArray(input)` tells the array apart from the string.
`input.split(",")` turns the string into an array, so both cases end up as a `string[]`.
Finish with one `map` that calls `trim()` and then `toLowerCase()` on every tag.

steps.title: null and undefined: ?., ??, and !

examples.title: Optional chaining with a default
examples.prompt: Print each customer's city and postcode, with defaults for the parts that are missing.
examples.output:
Ana: Lisbon, 1100-148
Ben: Leeds, no postcode
Caro: unknown city, no postcode
examples.explanation: Caro has no `address`, so `customer.address?.city` stops at `address` and gives `undefined`, and `??` puts `unknown city` in its place. Ben has an address without a postcode, so only his postcode falls back. With the defaults, `city` and `postcode` are plain strings, so the template literal never prints `undefined`.

examples.title: The ! lie
examples.prompt: Look up two prices with `!`, and one of the items isn't in the map.
examples.errorIncludes: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toFixed')
examples.explanation: `prices.get` returns `number | undefined`, and each `!` tells the checker to drop the `undefined`, so the file type-checks. There's no cup in the map, so `get("cup")` really is `undefined`, and calling `toFixed` on it throws. The mug line printed, then the program stopped before `done`. Press Run and the error shows the line with a space where the `!` was: Node stripped it like any other type.

examples.title: Handle it instead
examples.prompt: Look up the same prices, and print a clear message for an item that isn't for sale.
examples.output:
mug: 12.50
cup: not for sale
plate: 8.00
examples.explanation: Without a `!`, `price` is `number | undefined`, and the checker won't allow `price.toFixed` until you rule out `undefined`. The `if` handles the missing price and moves on with `continue`, so after it `price` is a `number`. The cup gets its own message, and the loop carries on to the plate.

practice.title: Customer city
practice.prompt:
Look up customers by id and print the city each one lives in.

1. For each id in `ids`, get the customer from the `customers` map.
2. When there is no customer with that id, print `<id>: no such customer`.
3. Otherwise print `<id>: <city>`, with `unknown` for a customer without an address.

Expected output:

```text
c1: Lisbon
c2: unknown
c9: no such customer
```

tests.output:
c1: Lisbon
c2: unknown
c9: no such customer

hints: `customers.get(id)` returns `Customer | undefined`. Rule out `undefined` before you read anything from it.
Print the missing customer's line and `continue`, the way the prices example does.
For the city, `customer.address?.city ?? "unknown"` handles a customer without an address.

recap:
- `A | B` accepts either type, and until you narrow it you can use only what both have.
- `typeof` narrows primitives, `===` narrows to a value, and an early `return` narrows the rest of the function.
- Truthiness removes `null` and `undefined` but also `""` and `0`, so compare with `undefined` or `null` when those count.
- `"key" in value`, `instanceof`, and `Array.isArray` narrow objects, classes, and arrays.
- `a?.b ?? fallback` reads data that may be missing and gives it a default.
- `value!` silences the checker without checking anything. Handle the missing case instead.
